video_title: The PAC taking out clean energy opponents
gist: Tom Matzzie, chair of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC, explains how a small, unpredictable PAC defeated anti-renewable Republicans like Chip Roy, Andy Ogles and Ralph Norman in 2026 primaries in order to give clean energy 'mythic power' with Congress. He describes the industry's structural weakness in politics (public affairs spending far below the roughly 2% of capex typical of mature industries, foreign ownership limits under FARA, and thin project-finance cash flow) and the PAC's next steps: targeting House Freedom Caucus-aligned candidates in the general election and copying ethanol's Iowa playbook in the 2028 presidential primaries.

insights.claim: The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition (ITC) super PAC, formed after the Republican budget bill gutted wind and solar tax credits, helped defeat Reps. Chip Roy, Andy Ogles and Ralph Norman (twice) plus Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee in 2026 primaries.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Clean energy now has a demonstrated electoral stick, which may change how lawmakers vote on renewable credits, permitting and energy policy.

insights.claim: Tom Matzzie says ITC intervened in six primary elections in 2026 and won all six, without anything close to a $200 million war chest.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: A relatively small spend got outsized political results, so the industry's political influence can rise faster than its fundraising.
insights.quote: we intervened in six elections and we're successful on all six so far during the primaries

insights.claim: ITC is putting another $15 million into seven House general-election races in fall 2026 and expects to be in more than 15 races in total once undisclosed governor races are included.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Midterm results will test whether the PAC's influence holds up in general elections, where money buys less.

insights.claim: In the Tennessee 5th District primary ITC outspent both campaigns and all other independent groups combined, while Andy Ogles had raised only $60,000 for his reelection against ITC's roughly $2 million.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Underfunded incumbents in low-turnout primaries are cheap targets, so a few million dollars can decide a race.
insights.quote: We have $2 million, he has $60,000.

insights.claim: Matzzie claims ITC defeated Andy Ogles even though Donald Trump campaigned for him, making it what he believes is the only group to beat a Trump-backed candidate in a primary this cycle; Trump disavowed Ogles the next day.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: A Trump endorsement does not fully protect weak candidates, which lowers the political risk of targeting them.

insights.claim: ITC's primary attacks mostly avoided energy and in several races charged Republican incumbents with not being loyal enough to Trump or 'MAGA enough,' hitting candidates on their existing weak spots.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Issue-based industry PACs can win by using whatever message moves voters, not by arguing their own policy issue.
insights.quote: our charge against the incumbent Republicans that they were not loyal enough to Donald Trump. That they were not MAGA enough for Texas.

insights.claim: The PAC was started by Peter Davidson and Brendan Bell of Line Climate Capital after the 2025 tax credit defeat, with investor Chris Larsen, who also invests in crypto, among its largest funders, and Tusk Strategies running strategy and PR.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Funding comes mainly from climate investors and one large donor, not from operating companies, so the effort could be fragile if that donor stops.

insights.claim: Matzzie's theory of change is that how powerful an industry is perceived to be matters more than its real resources, so the PAC is built to tell a story about the clean energy industry's power rather than about clean energy itself.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Investors should judge sector political risk partly by whether lawmakers fear the industry, not only by its economics.
insights.quote: The perception actually matters more than anything. The metaphor I use is you have to be a lion and not a gazelle.

insights.claim: ITC treats the other 435 members of Congress as the real audience: defeating one opponent in public is meant to change how all the others vote, following the Machiavellian idea of making an example of one enemy.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Look for second-order effects, such as softer anti-renewable rhetoric and fewer sign-on letters, rather than just counting wins.
insights.quote: You don't need to hang all of your enemies, just one of them in the public square.

insights.claim: ITC sees unpredictability as a key part of its deterrent: chiefs of staff should warn members that someone might drop $2 million into their next race if they attack clean energy.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: A credible, unpredictable threat could reduce anti-clean-energy legislative activity, which supports policy stability for renewables.
insights.quote: there might be somebody who drops $2 million into your next election if you do this

insights.claim: ITC times its races to put a story about its wins in the news every week or two, and it runs 'Don't Mess With Solar' ads in Washington DC's airport and transit system aimed at congressional staff and political media.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: The campaign targets Washington insiders, so its effect shows up in congressional behavior, not public opinion.

insights.claim: Matzzie welcomes targeted candidates complaining about the PAC, like Chip Roy posting on X or Ralph Norman spending half his concession speech on super PACs, because it spreads word of ITC's power to other lawmakers.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Public backlash from targets increases the deterrent, so loud criticism is a sign the strategy is working.
insights.quote: We love it when they do that. Cuz they're telling other members of Congress about us.

insights.claim: Matzzie argues a reputation for power lasts long after the wins stop, noting that the NRA is still feared even though it last defeated someone in the 1990s, but says keeping it up needs steady investment.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: A few years of visible wins could give clean energy lasting political leverage if funding continues.
insights.quote: when was the last time the NRA defeated somebody in election? It was the 1990s.

insights.claim: Matzzie says a fight comes before friendship in politics: after his group helped Ned Lamont beat Joe Lieberman in the 2006 Democratic primary, Senate Democratic leaders asked the next day whether they were still friends.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Showing strength can make opponents more willing to work with the industry, which goes against the industry's 'be everyone's friend' approach.
insights.quote: you actually by being strong and demonstrating your strength, you make it desirable that people want to be your friend

insights.claim: ITC's general-election targeting roughly shadows the House Freedom Caucus's announced investments, going after candidates, including in open seats, who are likely to join the caucus or who campaign against clean energy.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: How big the House Freedom Caucus gets after the midterms is a key signal for future votes on renewable credits and permitting.

insights.claim: Matzzie blames House Freedom Caucus members Ralph Norman, Chip Roy and Andy Harris for going to the White House and asking President Trump to stop clean energy permits, which led to the administration's actions against the industry.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: A small group of lawmakers pushed the executive-branch permitting freeze, so changes to that group's influence affect federal permitting risk for renewables.
insights.quote: Ralph Norman went on television to brag about how he was getting the president to stop permits.

insights.claim: ITC picks races based on whether it can make an impact: it skips heavily funded marquee races and favors weak candidates with problems like bombastic comments or a falsified biography.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: The PAC's targets are likely to be lower-profile races where its money matters most.

insights.claim: Based on running independent expenditures in the 2006 wave, Matzzie predicts Democrats will underperform in the most-hyped, heavily funded 2026 House races, with most wins coming from races that became competitive in recent months or late in the campaign.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: When forecasting midterm control, look past headline races to second-tier and late-breaking districts.
insights.quote: the Democrats will underperform in those races

insights.claim: Matzzie says money goes much further in primaries than in general elections because most general-election voters stay in their partisan camps and very few can be persuaded.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Expect the PAC's general-election win rate and per-dollar impact to be lower than in the primaries.

insights.claim: Charlie Hatcher, the Republican nominee who replaced Andy Ogles in Tennessee's 5th District, spoke about clean energy in a moderate way, opposing subsidies the same way he opposes farm subsidies rather than using culture-war language. Matzzie reads this as an early sign of behavioral change.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Softer Republican rhetoric on clean energy would be an early sign of lower policy risk for renewables.

themes.theme: Why clean energy is politically weak

insights.claim: Matzzie says mature industries spend about 2% of capex on public affairs, while clean energy spends only a fraction of a tenth of a percent.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: The industry spends far too little on political influence, which helps explain why tax credits could be repealed with no consequences.
insights.quote: Fractions of a tenth of a percent.

insights.claim: Matzzie says industries usually mature politically only in their fourth or fifth decade, and clean energy has to do it faster because opponents are actively trying to hurt it.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Expect clean energy's political spending and organization to grow over the coming years.

insights.claim: Clean energy companies are structurally limited in political spending: many big US operators are foreign-owned or owned by foreign pension funds and FARA bars them from funding super PACs, while 6-8% project returns and project finance send cash flow to debt service and tax equity instead of the company.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Structural limits, not just culture, keep the industry's political spending low, so do not expect that to change quickly.
insights.quote: We build on 6, 7, 8%returns.

insights.claim: ITC's donor base is dozens of executives giving $50,000 to $100,000 each plus a few companies funding its 501(c)(4) arm, not companies writing seven-figure checks, partly because the industry has produced few billionaires compared with crypto, oil and gas, tech or AI.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Clean energy's political spending is still small next to crypto or fossil fuels, which limits its sway with party leaders.

insights.claim: Matzzie says clean energy lacks the local relationship network that groups like the Realtors, pharmacists, insurance brokers and community bankers have in every congressional district, and he sees that as the industry's biggest political gap.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Expect industry efforts to build district-level advocacy, and look for policy gains where that local depth already exists.

insights.claim: North Carolina is Matzzie's model: because solar is part of rural economic development there and the industry invested in relationships, the legislature passed a bipartisan climate bill with real solar and clean energy build-out targets.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: States where solar is part of rural economies, like North Carolina and Georgia, have more durable bipartisan support for renewables.

insights.claim: Matzzie says IRA investment in Republican areas was a sound strategy that did not have enough time to work and was not spread across enough districts, though Georgia shows it can build support; the industry still cannot rely on it alone.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Bets on red-state manufacturing reducing political risk are slow; pair them with direct political pressure.
insights.quote: It's like deciding you're going to grow your own garden for all the food you eat this year

insights.claim: Matzzie says Americans agree with clean energy but it is not popular the way the iPhone is: people want working lights and moderate bills, and that agreement does not become political enthusiasm.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Favorable polling on renewables overstates their political protection, so do not treat agreement as support that wins votes.
insights.quote: there's difference between agreement and popularity

insights.claim: Matzzie says the clean energy trade associations, SEIA and American Clean Power Association, have little real electoral strategy, and their PACs reportedly split giving between parties, including to some members who voted to kill the tax credits.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Trade group PAC giving has bought little protection, which is why an independent accountability group is now active.

insights.claim: Matzzie says SEIA, under new leader Tim Pawlenty, changed its message within the last 48 hours to call for 'a stick and a carrot' instead of just making friends.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Trade groups may be moving toward a more confrontational stance, a sign of a broader political change in the industry.

insights.claim: Matzzie says an aggressive PAC should stay outside the trade associations so that Speaker Mike Johnson cannot ask SEIA's leader to call it off; he says that distance and deniability are part of the strategy.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Separating lobbying from accountability keeps both channels working and makes the threat harder to negotiate away.
insights.quote: I'll take their phone call, but I'm not going to take their orders.

insights.claim: David Roberts argues American Clean Power Association is about half gas, because diversified members like NextEra own large fossil fleets, so no trade group pushes policies that replace gas with clean electricity.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Clean energy policy advocacy is weakened by members' gas interests, which slows policies that shift load from gas to electricity.

insights.claim: Matzzie admits the clean energy trade groups are not working on expanding total electricity demand, such as electrification and home-heating standards, and suggests SEIA, which has no utility members, is best placed to take it on, possibly with the Edison Electric Institute.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Electrification policy has no strong industry champion yet, which is a gap for long-term electricity demand growth.
insights.quote: total addressable market is a very important part of our industry's long-term success

insights.claim: Matzzie praises NextEra as the largest US clean energy investor, with impressive internal deployment technology, but says its national public affairs presence is very small compared with its competitors, except inside Florida.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Even the sector leader underinvests in politics, which shows how far industry-wide spending has to rise.

insights.claim: Matzzie says the clean energy industry is united behind the pending permitting bill expected in the lame-duck session, while green groups are less supportive, and ITC would consider going after leaders who derail it.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Passing permitting reform in the lame duck is a key catalyst for renewable developers; watch the vote and who blocks it.
insights.quote: Oil and gas has not had any difficulty in building everything they want to build. This is not the case for clean energy.

insights.claim: Matzzie says Trump retaliates against people who attack him personally but has not punished good-faith industry advocacy, citing offshore wind, which won about five court cases through regional trade groups with no retribution and is now part of permitting negotiations.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Companies may be overestimating the political risk of standing up for themselves; offshore wind getting into the permitting talks is a possible upside to watch.
insights.quote: Trump respects strength, not weakness.

insights.claim: Roberts notes that the administration has frozen permitting for solar and wind on public lands and that offshore wind has been hit hard, which Matzzie calls wreckage from a temporary political moment.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Federal permitting risk for projects on public lands and offshore remains severe in the near term.

insights.claim: ITC plans to copy the ethanol industry's Iowa strategy in the 2028 presidential primaries, organizing wind and solar families in early states like Iowa, Michigan, South Carolina and Nevada to press candidates such as J.D. Vance, Marco Rubio, Kamala Harris or Gavin Newsom.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Presidential candidates' positions on wind and solar could shift if early-state organizing works, as ethanol did for the RFS.
insights.quote: I'm a wind farm family, I'm a solar farm family t-shirts

insights.claim: Matzzie says ITC wants to avoid being seen as Democratic-aligned and will look for Democratic primary targets, noting that as a solar developer he found local Democrats were sometimes the main obstacle.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Local opposition to projects from Democrats is a real risk; a bipartisan accountability threat would cover project-level NIMBY politics in blue areas too.

insights.claim: Matzzie says the clean energy industry needs a much larger industry-wide investment in public affairs, including state and local relationships and communications, because non-economic barriers like community engagement are now limiting deployment and no single company can fund this alone.
insights.speaker: Tom Matzzie
insights.so_what: Non-economic barriers are now a main limit on deployment; companies that manage community and political relationships well may deploy faster.
insights.quote: we have non-economic barriers to deployment
